introduction-beyond-the-browser.core: WebAssembly is a portable, compact binary instruction format with a sandboxed, capability-free execution model, designed for browsers but now used server-side. Wasm modules start in microseconds to milliseconds, are tiny, run on any CPU architecture via a runtime and can't touch anything the host doesn't explicitly grant.

first_principles.problem: Serverless and edge platforms want stronger isolation and faster startup than containers can offer.
truths: A small, well-defined VM is easy to sandbox.
derivation: Compile languages (Rust, Go, C, C#…) to **.wasm**.

analogy.title: A universal game cartridge
analogy.story: It runs on any console with the right slot, and can't touch the console's other games.
analogy.breaks: Cartridges contain hardware; Wasm modules are pure bytecode interpreted or compiled by the runtime.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One binary runs on x86 and ARM hosts.

code.text:
rustup target add wasm32-wasip2
cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip2
wasmtime target/wasm32-wasip2/release/hello.wasm

check.q: Why is Wasm considered secure by default?
check.a: Modules can't access host resources unless the runtime explicitly grants capabilities.

the-missing-link-wasi.core: Wasm itself has no I/O. WASI (WebAssembly System Interface) defines standard, capability-based APIs for files, clocks, random numbers, sockets and HTTP, so modules can do server-side work. WASI Preview 2 and the Component Model add typed interfaces (WIT) so components in different languages can compose.

first_principles.problem: A Wasm module can compute but can't read a file or open a socket.

analogy.title: A visitor pass listing exactly which rooms you may enter
analogy.story: You can't wander; doors open only if they're on your pass.
analogy.breaks: Passes can be forged; WASI capabilities are enforced by the runtime.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Module can read /data and nothing else.

code.text: wasmtime run --dir ./data::/data app.wasm   # only ./data visible as /data

check.q: What does WASI add to WebAssembly?
check.a: Standard capability-based system interfaces like files, clocks, sockets and HTTP.

wasm-vs-containers-architecture-deep-div.core: Containers package an OS userland and run native processes on a shared kernel; Wasm modules are architecture-neutral bytecode executed in a runtime sandbox. Wasm is smaller (KB–MB), starts faster (µs–ms) and is deny-by-default, but has a less mature ecosystem, limited threading and syscall support and different debugging. Containers run anything Linux can.

first_principles.problem: Teams wonder whether Wasm will replace containers.
derivation: **Containers** for general workloads and existing apps.
**Wasm** for fast-start, high-density, untrusted or portable functions.
Run Wasm on Kubernetes via **runwasi shims/SpinKube**.

analogy.title: A furnished apartment versus a hotel capsule
analogy.story: The apartment fits any lifestyle; the capsule is tiny, instant to check into, and limited.
analogy.breaks: Capsules can't host big families; Wasm can't yet run arbitrary Linux software.

example.title: Size and startup
flow: Container: 80 MB image, ~500 ms cold start
Density: thousands of modules per host

check.q: Name one reason Wasm won't replace containers soon.
check.a: Its ecosystem is less mature, with limited support for threads, syscalls and arbitrary existing software.

wasm-on-the-edge-the-speed-advantage.core: Edge platforms (Cloudflare Workers, Fastly Compute, Fermyon, Akamai) run Wasm or V8 isolates at hundreds of locations. Microsecond-to-millisecond instantiation means no cold starts worth noticing, tiny memory per tenant allows massive multi-tenancy, and the sandbox safely runs customer code close to users.

first_principles.problem: Containers at the edge cost too much memory and have cold starts longer than the request itself.

analogy.title: Pop-up stalls that appear the moment a customer arrives
analogy.story: No setup wait, and they vanish when the customer leaves.
analogy.breaks: Stalls carry stock; edge functions need external storage for state.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Auth in ~5 ms near the user.

check.q: Why are Wasm cold starts rarely an issue at the edge?
check.a: Instantiating a Wasm module takes microseconds to milliseconds.

the-developer-experience-runtimes-and-fr.core: The Wasm developer stack: languages with strong targets (Rust first-class, Go/TinyGo, C/C++, C#, JS/Python via embedded interpreters), runtimes (Wasmtime, WasmEdge, Wasmer, WAMR), frameworks (Spin, wasmCloud) that add HTTP triggers, KV and messaging, and Kubernetes integration (SpinKube, runwasi). Tooling for debugging and profiling is improving but less mature than for containers.

first_principles.problem: A team tries Wasm and struggles to find which language, runtime and framework to use.

analogy.title: An emerging city's infrastructure
analogy.story: Main roads are excellent, side streets are still being paved.
analogy.breaks: Cities take decades; the Wasm ecosystem moves yearly.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: HTTP service as a Wasm component in minutes.

code.text:
spin new -t http-rust hello
cd hello && spin build && spin up
# curl localhost:3000 → Hello from Wasm
